newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton prices seen easing in Pakistan and India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton prices seen easing in Pakistan and India.

text.p: Cotton prices are likely to fall in the coming week in Pakistan and India as fresh crop supplies rise, dealers in the two countries said on Thursday.
Karachi dealers said prices rose in the week to Thursday on rumours of massive crop damage from pest attacks in the main growing central province of Punjab.
But government officials said Pakistan would still achieve its production target of 10 million 375-lb bales for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) as the damage had been "limited".
"There has been some damage but the situation is not alarming at the moment," Zahoor Ahmed, director of the state-run Cotton Research Institute told Reuters by telephone from Multan.
On Thursday Karachi Cotton Association spot rates, including a 10 percent sales tax, held steady as panic-striken spinners slowed down buying after official denials of major crop damage.
KCA spot NIAB-78 was steady at 2,416 rupees ($65.19) per maund (37.32 kg) and for MNH-93 at 2376.50 rupees. On the kerb, NIAB-78 traded in the 2,200-2,120 range, dealers said.

In India, lower demand by cotton millers and improved arrivals pushed down cotton prices last week, traders said.
"Mill demand was low while improved supplies triggered unloading by stockists as well as state-owned agencies," one dealer said.
Daily new-crop arrivals in the northern state of Punjab rose to 7,000 to 8,000 bales (170 kg each) and could rise further.
"New crop arrivals have also commenced in central and western India but daily inflow remains thin," one trader said.
In spot deals during the week, Gujarat Kalyan fell 400/700 rupees to 12,800/12,900 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) while waged cotton moved down to 10,800/10,900 rupees from 11,500.
Bengal-deshi ready delivery slid 40 rupees to 830/850 rupees per maund while November delivery fell 30/35 rupees to 870/890.
New Punjab saw-ginned cotton slipped to 1,610/1,660 rupees from 1,625/1,675 rupees per maund during the week.
The Indian 1995/96 cotton crop, which ended in September, was 15.65 million bales compared with 13.85 million in 1994/95.
India's 1996/97 cotton-growing area is likely to be three to four percent above the 8.31 million hectares in 1995/96, Cotton Corporation of India chairman M.B. Lal said.
The government allowed exports of 150,000 bales of cotton in 1996/97. More export quota may be released after receiving a clear picture of the new crop, one trader said.
